payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
The open question I left at the end of what it would take to make signing routine was cost at the point of creation. Nobody has priced making a signature free, automatic and invisible in the moment a record gets made. Most of that experiment has already run once, and the results are public.

What was actually built

Session, founded in 2019 by Björn Ulvaeus, Max Martin and Niclas Molinder out of the earlier Auddly, shipped a tool called Session Studio that embedded inside digital audio workstations, the software a record is assembled in. It captured song and contributor data as the work happened rather than reconstructing it later. It cost nothing to use. Grants from Spotify and YouTube funded it. SoundCloud wired up to receive audio and metadata directly from the app in October 2022, the Brazilian collection society UBC followed that December, and TuneCore began distributing from it in August 2023.

That is close to the configuration the argument assumes. Free, sitting where the work happens, with a distributor and a society on the other end. The tool did not become the default way records get documented.

The ceiling nobody removed

Session Studio confirmed collaborator identity through performing rights organizations, the bodies that register songwriters and collect their royalties. Anyone holding a membership could be verified. Everyone else had no route in, which is the boundary I wrote about in who gets vouched for and it does not move because the software got cheaper. A session player working under a handle, a producer between deals, an artist in a market where affiliation is rare: all of them can operate the tool and none of them can be verified by it. The people whose money most often goes missing sit outside the roster that defines who counts.

There is a second thing the design never handed back. A contributor filling in that record produced an asset held by the company, and the company changed hands in March 2023 when Salt, a royalty processing platform selling back-office systems to collecting societies, acquired it. Nothing was lost in that transaction. Nothing was portable either.

What one case can carry

A single deployment does not prove a law, and this one comes with confounds no outside reading can separate. The tool arrived before AI made documentation urgent. Session's founders had enormous industry standing, which cuts both ways as evidence. Whatever internal numbers exist have never been published.

What the case does establish is narrower and still useful. Removing cost was tried, at real scale, with distribution and society integration already in place, and cost turned out not to be the binding constraint. That answers half of the question I left open and replaces it with a better one. The variable nobody has tested is what the contributor holds at the end. Every deployment so far has asked people to document their work and given them a record kept somewhere else, verified against a membership they may not have. A key held by the contributor changes both of those at once, and no one has run that version long enough to find out whether the trade reads differently from the other side.

References

payload.title: The free version already shipped
